opus-5.5.text:
I think it's changed a lot, and honestly not always in the direction I'd hoped. When I started working on this a few years ago, there was this sense that the norm in the field was openness. You'd publish a paper, you'd release the code, often the model weights, and you'd describe your training data in a reasonable amount of detail. That wasn't perfect, but it was the default expectation.

What we've seen since then, especially with large language models becoming commercially valuable, is a real retreat from that. Some of the biggest model releases now come with what are essentially technical reports that tell you very little: nothing about the training data, nothing about the compute used, nothing about the energy or the carbon footprint. And that's a problem, because you can't evaluate what you can't see. You can't audit a model for bias if you don't know what it was trained on, and you can't compare environmental costs if nobody reports them.

At the same time, there's been a really encouraging counter-movement. You have open-source communities, initiatives like BigScience with BLOOM, where we tried to document everything, from the data governance to the carbon emissions of training. You have things like model cards and datasheets becoming more standard, and more people in the community saying, "If you want us to take your claims seriously, show your work." And regulators are starting to pay attention too, asking questions about disclosure, especially around energy use and data provenance.

So I'd say transparency has become more polarized. There's a part of the field that's more transparent than ever, and a part that's become much more closed. My hope is that the pressure from researchers, users and policymakers pushes things back toward openness, because I really believe we can't make AI more sustainable or more ethical if we don't even have the basic information about how these systems are built.

r001.rationale: The response describes reduced disclosure in some commercially valuable model releases, but does not say that scientific AI conferences now accept papers with less model disclosure than they required a few years ago.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think transparency has moved in two directions at once, and that's what makes it such an interesting question right now.

On one hand, we've seen enormous progress in the open ecosystem. When I started in this field, sharing model weights, datasets, and training code was something you did if you were feeling generous. Now there's a whole community that treats it as the default, and tooling like model cards and dataset documentation has gone from being a niche academic proposal to something people actually expect to see. The fact that we can now have real conversations about what's in a training set, or how much energy a model consumed, is because people pushed for that documentation to exist.

On the other hand, the frontier has gotten much more opaque. The biggest, most capable models are increasingly released with a technical report that tells you almost nothing about the data, the compute, or the carbon footprint. We went from papers that listed every hyperparameter to announcements that won't even confirm the parameter count. And that's partly competitive pressure, partly legal caution around data provenance, and partly a safety narrative that gets invoked, sometimes genuinely and sometimes conveniently.

So my concern is that we've created a two-tier system. Smaller labs and academic groups are held to quite high transparency standards, while the organizations with the most societal impact disclose the least. And the environmental side is where I feel this most sharply, because you can't audit what you can't measure. If a company won't tell you how much compute went into training, you can't estimate emissions, you can't compare approaches, and you can't hold anyone accountable.

What gives me some hope is regulation starting to catch up, and the fact that researchers have gotten creative about measurement from the outside. But I'd say we're at a moment where transparency is being renegotiated rather than steadily improving, and the outcome really isn't settled yet.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier model releases disclose less than earlier papers, but it does not claim that scientific AI conferences now accept papers with less model disclosure.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s changed quite a bit, and not necessarily for the better. A few years ago, there was more of an expectation that, if you published a model, you would explain how you trained it, what data you used, and how you evaluated it. That didn’t mean everything was perfectly transparent, but sharing those details was part of the research process.

Now, as AI has become more commercially valuable, we’re seeing less disclosure about some of the most widely used systems. You can interact with a model, but you may know very little about what went into it. And that makes it difficult to reproduce results or independently assess things like bias and environmental impact.

There are still researchers and communities pushing for openness. But I think we need to be more precise about what transparency means. Releasing model weights is useful, but it doesn’t tell you the whole story. We also need documentation about the data, the training process, and the limitations so that people can actually scrutinize these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says disclosure by AI companies and model developers has declined, but it does not claim scientific AI conferences now accept papers with less model disclosure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve seen a shift toward less transparency, especially as models have become more commercially valuable. A few years ago, sharing your research often meant sharing the code, the data, and enough detail for someone else to reproduce it. Now, you might get a technical report that tells you how well a model performs, but very little about what went into it.

And transparency isn’t just about releasing model weights. It’s also about documenting the training data, the resources used, the limitations, and the evaluations. Without that information, it’s really difficult for independent researchers to understand these systems or hold their developers accountable.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general shift toward less transparency in AI research, but does not say that scientific AI conferences now accept papers with less model disclosure than they required a few years ago.
